client.label: HTTP client
client.headers: Request headers, one Name: value per line
client.empty: Send a request to see what the server answers.
client.noResponse: No response: the request is still waiting. Every route must end with `res.send()`, `res.json()`… or call `next()`.
client.timeout: No response after {{seconds}} s: the request was given up.
client.stopped: The server is stopped: fix the error shown in the server log, it restarts as soon as your code runs.

log.title: Server log
log.empty: Nothing yet. Requests, `console.log` output and errors show up here.

notices.databaseFailed: The database could not be loaded: reload the page.

errors.infiniteLoop: This loop never ends: it was stopped after {{count}} turns. Check its condition.
errors.noApp: There is no app: create one with `const app = express()`.

routes.name: app.get
routes.definition: A route tells the server what to answer to a request: `app.get(path, (req, res) => { … })` runs the function for every GET request on that path. `req` is the request received, `res` the response to send.

json.name: res.json
json.definition: `res.json(value)` turns a value into JSON text and sends it, with the `Content-Type: application/json` header that tells the client how to read it. JSON is the language most APIs speak.

collection.name: GET /bricks
collection.definition: A REST API gives every kind of thing a URL: the collection `/bricks` holds every brick, `/bricks/1` is one of them. A GET request reads, it never changes anything.

query.name: req.query
query.definition: The query string is the part of the URL after `?`: `/bricks?color=red&max=10`. Express reads it into `req.query`, an object whose values are always text. It's the usual way to filter, sort or search.

params.name: req.params
params.definition: A route parameter is a part of the path that changes: in `app.get('/bricks/:id', …)`, `/bricks/3` gives `req.params.id === '3'`. Like everything in a URL, it is text.

status.name: res.status
status.definition: Every response has a status code: `200` OK, `201` created, `204` nothing to send back, `400` bad request, `404` not found, `500` the server failed. `res.status(404)` sets it before sending.

post.name: POST
post.definition: POST sends data to the server to create something new. The data travels in the request body, as JSON; `app.use(express.json())` reads it into `req.body`. The answer is `201 Created`, with what was created.

validation.definition: Never trust what a client sends. Check the body before using it, and answer `400 Bad Request` with an explanation when it's wrong: nothing is saved.

put.name: PUT
put.definition: PUT replaces a whole resource with the one sent in the body: `PUT /bricks/1` sends a complete brick. The id comes from the URL, not from the body.

patch.name: PATCH
patch.definition: PATCH changes only some fields of a resource: `PATCH /bricks/1` with `{ "stock": 0 }` changes the stock and keeps everything else.

delete.name: DELETE
delete.definition: DELETE removes a resource: `DELETE /bricks/3`. There is nothing left to send back, so the answer is `204 No Content`, without a body.

rest.name: REST
rest.definition: A REST API names things, not actions: plural nouns (`/bricks`), ids in the path (`/bricks/1`), related things nested (`/bricks/1/orders`). The action is the HTTP method: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE.

middleware.name: next()
middleware.definition: A middleware is a function `(req, res, next)` that runs before the routes, added with `app.use`. It answers itself, or calls `next()` to hand the request to what comes next. If it does neither, the request waits forever.

auth.definition: An API protects its writes: the client proves who it is in a header, like `X-API-Key`. Without it, `401 Unauthorized`; with a wrong one, `403 Forbidden`. A middleware given to a route checks it before the handler.

errors.name: (err, req, res, next)
errors.definition: An error handler is a middleware with four parameters, added after the routes. Express calls it when a route throws or calls `next(error)`. It logs the details for you and sends the client a short message.

database.name: await db.all
database.definition: A database keeps the data when the server restarts. Its calls take time, so they return promises: inside an `async` function, `await db.all(sql)` waits for every row, `await db.get(sql)` for the first one.

placeholders.definition: A placeholder `?` in the SQL stands for a value given apart, in an array: `db.all('… WHERE color = ?', [color])`. The database never reads the value as SQL, which blocks SQL injection.

insert.name: db.run
insert.definition: `await db.run(sql, params)` runs an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. It resolves with `changes`, the number of rows changed, and `lastInsertRowid`, the id the database gave to the last row inserted.

changes.name: result.changes
changes.definition: UPDATE and DELETE change every row their `WHERE` matches: without `WHERE`, every row. `result.changes` tells how many rows changed: 0 means nothing matched, so the resource doesn't exist.

fetch.name: fetch
fetch.definition: In the browser, `fetch(url, options)` sends a request to an API and returns a promise of the response; `response.json()` reads its JSON body. The page and the API must agree on URLs, fields and status codes: that's the API contract.

hello.title: Say hello
intro: Welcome to the Brick Shop API! In every step you write the server of a toy brick shop, with Node.js and Express. Your code goes in `server.js` on the left; on the right, an HTTP client sends requests to your server and the server log shows what happens.

The first two lines create an app, the last one starts it on port 3000. In between come the routes: `app.get('/hello', handler)` runs `handler` for every GET request on `/hello`, and `res.send(text)` sends the answer.
hello.goal: Add a route so that `GET /hello` answers with the text `Brick Shop API`.
hints: The route goes between `const app = express()` and `app.listen(…)`, like the example below.
The text must be exactly `Brick Shop API`, between quotes: `res.send('Brick Shop API')`.
hello.recap: A route is a method (`get`), a path (`/hello`) and a function that answers with `res`. Any other method or path gets a `404`.

shop-info.title: Speak JSON
intro: Plain text is fine for a human, but programs need structure. APIs answer in JSON: the same objects you write in JavaScript, as text.
`res.json(value)` sends any object or array as JSON, with a `Content-Type: application/json` header. Open the Headers tab of the response to see it.
shop-info.goal: Make `GET /shop` answer the JSON object `{ name: 'Brick Shop', open: true }`.
hints: Replace `res.send(…)` with `res.json(…)`.
`open` is the boolean `true`, without quotes.
shop-info.recap: `res.json` sends data a program can read: `response.open` is a real `true`, not text.

list-bricks.title: List the bricks
intro: The shop sells bricks: they're in the `bricks` array. In a REST API, the whole collection lives at a plural URL, `/bricks`.
The route already exists, but its function never answers. Send it: the client shows what the request receives, and the server log shows the request waiting forever.
list-bricks.goal: Make `GET /bricks` answer with the 5 bricks of the array, as JSON.
hints: `res.json` takes arrays as well as objects.
One line is enough: `res.json(bricks)`.
list-bricks.recap: The collection URL `/bricks` returns the list. A route that never answers leaves the client waiting: every route must send something.

checks.same: The bricks are the ones of the array

filter-color.title: Filter by color
intro: A customer only wants red bricks. Instead of a new URL, the client adds a query string: `/bricks?color=red`. Express reads it into `req.query`: here `req.query.color` is `'red'`.
Without `?color=…`, `req.query.color` is `undefined`: then answer every brick, as before.
filter-color.goal: Make `GET /bricks?color=red` answer only the red bricks, and `GET /bricks` every brick.
hints: `bricks.filter((b) => b.color === color)` keeps the bricks of that color.
Use `if (color) { return res.json(…) }` before the last line, so that only one answer is sent.
filter-color.recap: `req.query` holds the filters of the URL. A filter that matches nothing is not an error: it's an empty list, `200 []`.

checks.unknown: An unknown color gives an empty list `[]`

one-brick.title: One brick
intro: Each brick has its own URL: `/bricks/2`. The route `/bricks/:id` matches them all, and Express puts the changing part in `req.params.id`.
This route looks right, but `GET /bricks/2` sends nothing back. Everything in a URL is text: `req.params.id` is `'2'`, and `2 === '2'` is false.
one-brick.goal: Fix the route so that `GET /bricks/2` answers the brick whose id is 2.
hints: `Number(req.params.id)` turns `'2'` into `2`.
Compare `b.id` with the number: `const id = Number(req.params.id)`.
one-brick.recap: `req.params` and `req.query` are always text: convert them with `Number()` before comparing them to numbers.

not-found.title: Not found
intro: Ask for `GET /bricks/99`: the answer is `200 OK`, with nothing inside. The client can't tell that the brick doesn't exist.
The status code tells it: `res.status(404).json(…)` sends a `404 Not Found`. Write `return` in front of it, so that the function stops there: a request gets one answer, never two.
not-found.goal: Answer `404` with `{ error: 'Brick not found' }` when the brick doesn't exist.
hints: `find` returns `undefined` when nothing matches: test it with `if (!brick) { … }`.
Without `return`, the code goes on to `res.json(brick)`, which tries to send a second answer: the server log shows the error.
not-found.recap: The status code is the first thing a client reads: `200` it worked, `404` it doesn't exist. `return res.status(…)…` ends the function after the answer.

checks.message: The body is `{ error: 'Brick not found' }`
checks.once: Only one answer is sent: no error in the log

create-brick.title: Create a brick
intro: To add a brick, the client sends a POST request to the collection, `/bricks`, with the new brick in the body, as JSON.

Express doesn't read the body by itself: until you add `app.use(express.json())` after `const app = express()`, `req.body` is `undefined`. The new brick then gets the next id, joins the array, and the answer is `201 Created` with the brick.
create-brick.goal: Make `POST /bricks` add the brick sent, with a new id, and answer `201` with it.
hints: Add `app.use(express.json())` right after `const app = express()`.
Build `{ id: nextId++, name: req.body.name, … }`, then `bricks.push(brick)`.
`res.status(201).json(brick)`.
create-brick.recap: POST on a collection creates. The server chooses the id, never the client, and `201` says that something new exists.

checks.returned: The answer is the new brick, with the id 6
checks.newIds: Two bricks get two ids: 6 and 7

validate.title: Refuse bad bricks
intro: Send `{ "color": "red", "price": 1 }`: a brick without a name joins the shop. Anything can arrive in a request: a field missing, text where a number is expected.
Check the body before using it. When it's wrong, answer `400 Bad Request` with an `error` that explains why, and save nothing.
validate.goal: Answer `400` with an `error` when the name is missing or the price is not a number.
hints: `typeof price !== 'number'` is true for `'cheap'` and for a missing price.
Test at the top of the function, and `return res.status(400).json({ error: '…' })`.
The check comes before `nextId++` and `push`: a refused brick takes no id.
validate.recap: Validate first, then act. `400` means the client must fix its request; the `error` tells it what to fix.

checks.noName: A brick without a name gets `400`
checks.badPrice: A price that is not a number gets `400`

replace-brick.title: Replace a brick
intro: To change a brick, PUT sends it whole to its URL: `PUT /bricks/1` with a name, a color, a price and a stock. The brick at that index is replaced by the one sent.
The id comes from the URL: even if the body holds another `id`, the brick keeps its own. And an unknown id is a `404`, like for GET.
replace-brick.goal: Make `PUT /bricks/:id` replace the brick with the body and answer it, or answer `404`.
hints: `findIndex` returns `-1` when nothing matches.
`{ ...req.body, id: bricks[index].id }` copies the body and puts the right id last, so it wins.
`bricks[index] = brick`, then `res.json(brick)`.
replace-brick.recap: PUT replaces the whole resource at a URL. The URL decides which one, so the id never comes from the body.

checks.sameId: An `id` in the body doesn't change the id

patch-brick.title: Change only the stock
intro: The brick 1 is sold out: the client only wants to send `{ "stock": 0 }`. Try it: this PATCH route rebuilds the brick from the body, and the name, color and price disappear.
PATCH changes only the fields sent. The spread operator merges two objects: `{ ...brick, ...req.body }` starts from the brick and lets the body overwrite what it holds.
patch-brick.goal: Make `PATCH /bricks/:id` change only the fields sent and keep the others.
hints: Replace the object built field by field with `{ ...brick, ...req.body }`.
Add `id: brick.id` at the end, so that the body can't change the id.
patch-brick.recap: PUT replaces, PATCH merges. With spread, the last object wins: `{ ...old, ...changes, id }`.

checks.twoFields: Two fields sent, two fields changed
checks.sameId: An `id` in the body doesn't change the id

delete-brick.title: Remove a brick
intro: The yellow plate is gone for good: `DELETE /bricks/3` removes it.
Once it's removed, there is nothing to send back: the answer is `204 No Content`, with an empty body. As always, an id that doesn't exist answers `404`.
delete-brick.goal: Make `DELETE /bricks/:id` remove the brick and answer `204`, or `404`.
hints: Find its index with `findIndex`, then `bricks.splice(index, 1)` removes it.
`res.status(204).send()` sends the status without a body.
delete-brick.recap: DELETE removes, `204` confirms with nothing to read. After it, `GET` on the same URL answers `404`.

checks.others: The other bricks are still there

brick-orders.title: Orders of a brick
intro: Someone wrote `GET /getOrdersOfBrick?brickId=1`. It works, but it's not REST: a verb in the URL, and the brick hidden in the query string.
In REST, URLs name things: the orders of the brick 1 are `/bricks/1/orders`, nested under the brick they belong to. The method already says the action: GET reads.
brick-orders.goal: Replace the route with `GET /bricks/:id/orders`, which answers `404` for an unknown brick.
hints: The id now comes from `req.params.id`, converted with `Number()`.
`bricks.some((b) => b.id === id)` tells whether the brick exists.
Remove the old route: a URL with a verb should not stay.
brick-orders.recap: Nouns in the URL, the action in the method. A brick with no orders answers `[]`; a brick that doesn't exist answers `404`.

logger.title: Log every request
intro: To know what the server does, it logs every request. Instead of a `console.log` in each route, one middleware runs before all of them: `app.use(fn)`.
Send a request: it logs, then waits forever. A middleware receives a third parameter, `next`: calling it hands the request to the next middleware or route.
logger.goal: Make the middleware log every request and then let the routes answer.
hints: Add `next` to the parameters: `(req, res, next)`.
Call `next()` after the `console.log`.
logger.recap: Middleware runs in the order of `app.use`, before the routes added after it. It either answers or calls `next()`.

checks.every: Every request is logged, even a `404`

api-key.title: Protect deletion
intro: Anyone can delete a brick. Writes need a key: the client sends it in a header, `X-API-Key: brick-secret`, and `req.get('x-api-key')` reads it.
The check lives in `requireKey`, a middleware given only to the DELETE route, before its handler. Without a key the answer is `401 Unauthorized`, with a wrong one `403 Forbidden`; reading stays open.
api-key.goal: Make `requireKey` answer `401` without a key, `403` with a wrong key, and go on with the right one.
hints: `const key = req.get('x-api-key')` is `undefined` when the header is missing.
`return res.status(401).json({ error: '…' })` stops before `next()`.
In the client, the Headers tab takes one `Name: value` per line.
api-key.recap: A middleware given to one route guards only that route. `401`: who are you? `403`: I know, and it's no.

checks.kept: Refused deletions delete nothing, `GET` stays open

error-handler.title: Handle errors
intro: `GET /bricks/1/price/USD` converts a price. Try `GBP`: the rate doesn't exist, the code throws, and Express answers `500` with the error itself. The client reads details about your code it should never see.
An error handler takes four parameters, `(err, req, res, next)`, and goes after the routes. Express calls it when a route throws: log `err` for you, send the client a short message.
error-handler.goal: Add an error handler that logs the error with `console.error` and answers `500` with `{ error: 'Something went wrong' }`.
hints: `app.use((err, req, res, next) => { … })`, after the route and before `app.listen`.
Express only sees an error handler when it has exactly four parameters: keep `next`, even unused.
`console.error(err.message)` then `res.status(500).json({ error: 'Something went wrong' })`.
error-handler.recap: One error handler, at the end, catches what every route throws. Details go to the log, the client gets a `500` and a short message.

checks.json: An unknown currency answers `500` with the JSON error
checks.noLeak: The answer shows nothing of the error

sql-list.title: Read the database
intro: An array lives in memory: restart the server and every change is gone. From now on, the bricks live in the SQLite database you know, with its `bricks` and `orders` tables, shown below the client.
`require('./db')` gives `db`. Its calls return promises: mark the function `async`, then `await db.all('SELECT …')` waits for the rows.
sql-list.goal: Make `GET /bricks` answer every row of the `bricks` table.
hints: Put `async` before `(req, res) =>`, then `const bricks = await db.all('SELECT * FROM bricks')`.
Remove the old array: the data now comes from the database.
sql-list.recap: The route doesn't change, the source does. `async` and `await` wait for the database without blocking the server.

checks.ten: The answer holds the 10 bricks of the table
checks.rows: The bricks are the rows of the table

sql-injection.title: Block SQL injection
intro: This route glues the color into the SQL. Ask for `?color=it's`: the quote breaks the query, `500`. Worse, `?color=x' OR '1'='1` turns the condition into one that is always true: every brick comes out. That's SQL injection.
The fix: write `?` where the value goes, and give the values apart, in an array. The database never reads them as SQL.
sql-injection.goal: Use a `?` placeholder so that the color can never change the query.
hints: The SQL becomes `'SELECT * FROM bricks WHERE color = ?'`.
The values come second: `db.all(sql, [color])`.
sql-injection.recap: Never build SQL with `+` or a template literal from what a client sends: always `?` and an array of values.

checks.injection: The injection gives `[]`, not every brick

sql-insert.title: Insert a brick
intro: Creating a brick is now an `INSERT`. `await db.run(sql, params)` runs it and resolves with `lastInsertRowid`, the id the database gave to the new row.
Answer with the brick as it's stored: read it back with `db.get` and that id.
sql-insert.goal: Make `POST /bricks` insert the brick and answer `201` with the stored row.
hints: `INSERT INTO bricks (name, color, price, stock) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)`, with `[name, color, price, stock]`.
`const result = await db.run(…)`, then `db.get('SELECT * FROM bricks WHERE id = ?', [result.lastInsertRowid])`.
sql-insert.recap: The database picks the id, `lastInsertRowid` tells which one. The new brick survives a restart of the server.

checks.newId: The new brick gets the id 11
checks.stored: The row is in the `bricks` table

sql-changes.title: Update with WHERE
intro: Send `PATCH /bricks/3` with a stock of 40 and look at the table: every brick now has 40. The `UPDATE` has no `WHERE`, so it changes every row.
`db.run` resolves with `changes`, the number of rows changed. With the right `WHERE`, 0 means no brick has that id: answer `404`.
sql-changes.goal: Change only the brick of the URL, and answer `404` when `PATCH` or `DELETE` change no row.
hints: `UPDATE bricks SET stock = ? WHERE id = ?`, with `[req.body.stock, req.params.id]`.
`if (result.changes === 0) { return res.status(404).json({ error: 'Brick not found' }) }`, in both routes.
sql-changes.recap: No `UPDATE` or `DELETE` without `WHERE`. `result.changes` turns "nothing matched" into a `404`.

shop-fetch.title: Open the shop
intro: The last piece: the shop page. Its code, in the `shop.js` tab, calls your API with `fetch`: it lists the bricks in stock and orders one with a click. It's fixed, so your API must give it exactly what it asks for.
Read it like a contract: which URL, which method, which fields it sends, which fields it reads in the answer. The page shows the result above the client.
shop-fetch.goal: Make the shop work: `GET /bricks?inStock=true` for the bricks in stock, `POST /orders` to store an order.
hints: `req.query.inStock` is the text `'true'`; then `WHERE stock > 0`.
The `orders` table needs `customer`, `brick_id`, `quantity` and `ordered_on`: `date('now')` gives today. Its `status` is `pending` by default.
Refuse a quantity below 1 with `400`, then answer `201` with the stored order: the page reads its `id` and `status`.
shop-fetch.recap: That's a full stack: the page fetches, the API validates and answers, the database keeps. Every step of this course is in this one.

checks.ordered: `POST /orders` answers `201` with the id 9 and the status `pending`
checks.stored: The order is in the `orders` table
